title: Buffer management
lead: Buffer-pool state, pin/unpin, replacement policies and DBMS control over page transfers.

sections.title: Buffer pool and pin/unpin
sections.html:
A buffer pool is a memory cache divided into frames, each holding a disk page. Metadata records the page ID, dirty flag and pin count for each frame. An in-memory lookup structure maps page IDs to frames.

pin(page) ensures the requested page is resident and increments its pin count. On a miss it selects a free frame or an unpinned victim, writes a dirty victim if necessary, reads the new page and returns its memory address. A frame with pin count greater than zero cannot be evicted.unpin(page, dirty) decrements the pin count and combines the supplied dirty flag with the existing flag using logical OR. Unpinning does not require immediate write-back. Pinning protects residency; concurrency control separately coordinates conflicting access, and recovery constrains write ordering.

PDF pp. 1–11

sections.title: LRU and CLOCK
sections.html:
A replacement policy chooses among unpinned frames. In the slides’ LRU policy, the manager tracks the last-unpin time and evicts the eligible frame with the oldest time. Maintaining exact recency can be expensive at high page-access rates.

CLOCK approximates recency with a reference bit per frame and a circular hand. An access sets the bit. During victim search, pinned frames are skipped; an unpinned frame with bit 1 has its bit cleared and receives another chance; an unpinned frame with bit 0 can be replaced. The hand advances as frames are examined.

The source trace replaces page 8 with page 10 after skipping pinned and recently referenced frames. Dirty-page write-back is a separate action from selecting the victim.

PDF pp. 12–21

sections.title: Sequential flooding and MRU
sections.html:
Sequential flooding occurs when a scan displaces pages that will be needed again before the scan ends. The source compares repeated scans of a six-page and a seven-page relation using six initially empty frames.

With six pages, LRU incurs six initial misses and then hits. With seven pages, requesting page 7 evicts page 1; the next pass requests page 1 and evicts page 2. This pattern continues, making every request a miss under the stated immediate-release scan assumptions.

MRU evicts the most recently used eligible page. In the source’s repeated-scan case, it preserves pages that will be reused earlier in the next pass. LRU, MRU and LRU-K exploit different access patterns; no policy is optimal for every workload.

PDF pp. 22–31

sections.title: Practical buffer management
sections.html:
The execution engine knows whether an access is a sequential scan, an index lookup or a repeated join input. It can provide priority hints, separate buffer pools for different page types and avoid treating every reference identically.

Prefetching requests upcoming pages before they are demanded. It can amortise storage overhead and overlap computation with I/O. Its usefulness depends on predicting pages that will actually be consumed.

The DBMS retains control rather than relying entirely on the operating-system cache because recovery requires controlled flushing and ordering, while query plans provide information useful to replacement and prefetching.

PDF pp. 32–35

quiz.question: P has dirty=true. What is dirty after unpin(P,false)?
options: It depends on the pin count
quiz.explanation: The new dirty flag is the old dirty flag OR the supplied dirty argument. true OR false remains true.
